titleText.es: Si soy un dios, ¿por qué Maru no es *mi* gato?
titleText.en: If I'm such a god, why isn't Maru *my* cat?
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish text is the exact title attribute in the Spanish archive; the English text is the exact official xkcd title attribute. The asterisks are part of both source strings.

regions.labelEs: UN PROCESADOR X64 FUNCIONA A MILES DE MILLONES DE CICLOS POR SEGUNDO PARA EJECUTAR EL KERNEL XNU, QUE SE DEBATE COMO UN LOCO A TRAVÉS DE TODA LA ABSTRACCIÓN POSIX PARA CREAR EL SISTEMA DARWIN QUE SUBYACE A OS X, QUE A SU VEZ SE ESFUERZA PARA CORRER FIREFOX Y SU RENDERIZADOR GECKO, QUE CREA UN OBJETO FLASH QUE MUESTRA DOCENAS DE FOTOGRAMAS CADA SEGUNDO.

excludedUnits.rationale: X64 is an unchanged processor-architecture label, not a Spanish lexical word.
XNU is the unchanged proper name of a software kernel, not a Spanish lexical word.
POSIX is an unchanged technical standard name, not a Spanish lexical word.
Darwin is the unchanged proper name of an operating-system foundation, not a Spanish lexical word in this context.
OS X is an unchanged operating-system product name, not Spanish lexical material.
Firefox is the unchanged browser product name, not a Spanish lexical word.
Gecko is the unchanged proper name of a software rendering engine, not a Spanish lexical word here.
Flash is the unchanged software platform name in this context, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Miles de millones de supplies the large quantity frame, and ciclos names what is being counted.
Para introduces the purpose, and ejecutar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Que points back to kernel, and se debate supplies the verb at the core of the added information.
Como un loco intensifies the manner of the struggle as frantic rather than describing a literal identity.
The three fixed words introduce movement through the layers that follow.
Para introduces the intended result, and crear stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Que points back to sistema, and subyace supplies the verb at the core of the added information.
Subyace is the present verb for one underlying system, and a introduces the named system above it.

applications.exampleEs: OS X, QUE A SU VEZ SE ESFUERZA
applications.explanationEn: The excluded product name is the thing being described; que opens the added information, and se esfuerza supplies its verb.
A su vez moves from one software layer to the next corresponding step in the chain.
Para introduces the purpose, and correr stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Que points back to renderizador, and crea supplies the verb at the core of the added information.
Que points back to objeto, and muestra supplies the verb at the core of the added information.
Docenas gives the approximate quantity, de links it to what is counted, and fotogramas names those counted images.

regions.labelEs: PORQUE QUERÍA VER A UN GATO SALTAR HACIA UNA CAJA Y CAERSE.

applications.explanationEn: Quería changes to express the past desire, while ver stays in its unchanged dictionary form as the desired action.
Quería uses the imperfect because it presents wanting as a past state that supplies background, not as one bounded event.
A marks the specific animate being receiving the seeing action, and un gato names that being.

applications.exampleEs: VER A UN GATO SALTAR HACIA UNA CAJA Y CAERSE
applications.explanationEn: Ver introduces the perception, a un gato names the observed being, and saltar and caerse are the two unchanged action verbs for what that being does.
Soy is a form of ser because un dios states the speaker's claimed identity rather than a location.

cards.noteEn: In computing, a procesador is the component that carries out instructions.

example.en: The processor runs the program.

cards.questionEn: Why does the long chain of computing layers make the cat-video punchline funny?
cards.answerEn: A huge, intricate stack of hardware and software work is reduced to the viewer's simple wish to watch a cat jump into a box and fall.
cards.noteEn: The chain moves from processor cycles through an operating-system kernel and compatibility layers to a browser, renderer, plug-in object, and video frames. Calling the viewer a god reverses the perspective: these complex layers serve an ordinary human request, even though the human does not directly control their details.
After a verb such as funcionar, a can introduce the speed or rate at which something operates.

example.es: La máquina funciona a cien ciclos por minuto.
example.en: The machine runs at one hundred cycles per minute.

cards.noteEn: Miles is the plural of mil when the number of thousands is not specified exactly.

example.en: Thousands of people arrived.

cards.questionEn: How does Spanish express thousands of millions of something—what English commonly calls billions?
cards.answerEn: Use miles de millones de, followed by the thing being counted.
cards.noteEn: Miles and millones stay plural, and de appears both between them and before the counted noun. In standard Spanish numbering, mil millones is one thousand million; English commonly calls that one billion.

example.es: La galaxia contiene miles de millones de estrellas.
example.en: The galaxy contains billions of stars.

cards.answerEn: of; or no separate English word, linking an amount to what it measures
cards.noteEn: After a quantity expression, de introduces the substance or thing being measured. English uses “of” in expressions such as a lot of or the amount of, but may leave de untranslated in others, such as un poco de agua, “a little water.”

example.en: I want a little water.

cards.noteEn: Millones is followed by de before the thing being counted.

example.en: There are millions of stars.

cards.noteEn: A ciclo is one repeated round in a process or machine.

example.en: The motor completes several cycles.

cards.noteEn: Before a unit of time, por can distribute an amount across each unit, corresponding to English “per” or “a”: por día, por semana, por noche.

example.en: I read one hour per day.

cards.noteEn: This noun names one second of time. It is separate from segundo meaning ‘second’ in an ordered list.

example.en: Wait one second.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.noteEn: In computing, ejecutar means making a program or set of instructions run. It has other senses, including carrying out a plan.

example.en: I am going to run the program.

cards.answerEn: kernel; core of an operating system
cards.noteEn: Kernel is a technical borrowing used in Spanish for the central software that manages hardware and basic system resources.

example.en: The kernel controls memory.

cards.questionEn: How do you add information about a named person or thing using “who,” “that,” or “which”?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the person or thing, then add a verb and the information about it.
cards.noteEn: Que links the added description to the person or thing before it. It does not change for masculine, feminine, singular, or plural nouns. The added part needs a verb: la casa que vimos means “the house that we saw.”

example.es: La casa que vimos es azul.
example.en: The house that we saw is blue.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks debatirse (‘struggle’)
cards.noteEn: Debatirse uses se as part of the verb when someone or something struggles against a difficulty. Se changes to me, te, nos, or os for other people.

example.es: La empresa se debate entre dos opciones.
example.en: The company struggles between two options.

cards.noteEn: With se, debate is a present form of debatirse used for one third-person subject. Here it describes effort and difficulty, not a verbal debate.

example.es: El nadador se debate contra la corriente.
example.en: The swimmer struggles against the current.

cards.noteEn: Unaccented como can introduce the person, thing, or situation used for a comparison. It does not ask “how”; the question word cómo has an accent.

example.en: She runs like her brother.

cards.promptEs: como un loco / como una loca
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone does something wildly, frantically, or ‘like crazy’ in informal Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Put como un loco after the action for a masculine subject, or como una loca for a feminine subject.
cards.noteEn: The expression intensifies the manner of an action rather than literally diagnosing anyone. The article and adjective change to una loca for a feminine subject and can become plural for a group.

example.es: Pedro buscó las llaves como un loco.
example.en: Pedro searched for the keys like crazy.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; part of a través de (“through”)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something goes or can be seen through something?
cards.answerEn: Use a través de before the thing: it means “through” or “across.”
cards.noteEn: Keep all three parts together. Before masculine singular el, de and el combine as del: a través del bosque. Before a feminine noun, use a través de la, as in a través de la ventana. The expression can describe literal passage or a figurative means.

example.es: La luz entra a través de la ventana.
example.en: The light comes in through the window.

cards.answerEn: part of a través de, “through” or “across”
no separate English word; completes a través de, “through”

cards.noteEn: In computing, an abstraction hides lower-level details behind a simpler interface or layer.

example.es: La biblioteca ofrece una abstracción sencilla.
example.en: The library provides a simple abstraction.

cards.noteEn: Subyace is the present form of subyacer used with one third-person subject. It often takes a before the thing supported or explained at a deeper level.

example.es: Una regla sencilla subyace al sistema.
example.en: A simple rule underlies the system.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that one idea, cause, or layer underlies something else?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of subyacer, then a, then the thing with that deeper basis.
cards.noteEn: Subyacer changes for the subject and time; a stays before the thing being supported or explained at a deeper level. A and el combine as al: subyace al problema.

example.es: Una causa común subyace a los dos errores.
example.en: A common cause underlies both errors.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; required after subyacer
cards.noteEn: Subyacer a algo places a before the thing that has the deeper basis. Before el, a and el combine as al.

example.en: That idea underlies the project.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins a su vez (‘in turn’)
cards.noteEn: A is fixed at the start of a su vez, an expression that moves to the next linked step or participant.

example.es: Marta avisó a Luis, que a su vez llamó a Ana.
example.en: Marta told Luis, who in turn called Ana.

cards.questionEn: How do you show that the next person or thing acts ‘in turn’ as part of a chain?
cards.answerEn: Use a su vez to introduce the corresponding next step or effect.
cards.noteEn: The three-word expression stays together. It often follows the person or thing taking the next turn, sometimes between commas, and can connect one cause or layer to the next.

example.es: Ana llamó a Luis, que a su vez avisó a Marta.
example.en: Ana called Luis, who in turn told Marta.

cards.answerEn: its; part of a su vez (‘in turn’)
cards.noteEn: Su is the possessive middle word in the fixed expression a su vez. The expression can refer to a person or thing taking its turn in a sequence.

example.es: El segundo equipo, a su vez, revisó los datos.
example.en: The second team, in turn, reviewed the data.

cards.answerEn: turn; part of a su vez (‘in turn’)
cards.noteEn: Vez ordinarily means a time or occasion. In a su vez, it helps mark the next corresponding step in a chain.

example.es: La lluvia llenó el río, que a su vez inundó el campo.
example.en: The rain filled the river, which in turn flooded the field.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks esforzarse (‘make an effort’)
cards.noteEn: Esforzarse uses se as part of the verb. Se changes to me, te, nos, or os for other people.

example.en: She makes an effort to learn.

cards.noteEn: With se, esfuerza is the present form of esforzarse used for one third-person subject.

example.en: Tomás makes an effort every day.

cards.noteEn: Su does not show the owner's gender. Here a singular institution or place is the owner.

example.en: The company changed its name.

cards.noteEn: In computing, a renderizador turns data or code into the visible image or output shown to a user.

example.en: The renderer creates the image.

cards.noteEn: Crea is the present form of crear used with one third-person subject or as a familiar positive command.

example.en: The program creates a file.

cards.noteEn: Objeto can name a physical item or, in computing, a unit of data and behavior.

example.en: The program saves each object.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that there are dozens of something?
cards.answerEn: Use docenas de before the thing being counted.
cards.noteEn: Docenas stays plural when it means an approximate large count. De is required before the following noun: docenas de cartas. The noun is normally plural when it names countable items.

example.en: We saw dozens of stars.

cards.noteEn: A fotograma is one still image in a film, animation, or video sequence.

example.es: El vídeo tiene treinta fotogramas por segundo.
example.en: The video has thirty frames per second.

cards.noteEn: Quería is a past form of querer used for a desire that existed at that past time. It does not say by itself whether the desire was fulfilled.

example.en: I wanted more time.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone wants to do?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of querer, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Querer changes to match the person and time, while the desired action stays unchanged: quiero salir, quieres comer, queremos dormir. Spanish does not insert a between the two verbs.

example.en: Lucía wants to rest.

cards.answerEn: Use the preterite for a completed event and the imperfect for background, an ongoing situation, or something that used to happen.
cards.noteEn: Think of a story: the preterite answers “What happened next?” The imperfect answers “What was happening?”, “What were things like?”, or “What used to happen?” These two names describe how the speaker presents an event, not simply how long it lasted.
cards.questionEn: Spanish has two common ways to talk about the past. When do you use each one?

example.en: While I was walking, it started to rain.

cards.promptEs: ver + persona o cosa + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that you see a person or thing perform an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of ver, name the person or thing observed, and put the observed action in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The plus signs show the order of the pieces. The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Only ver changes for the viewer and time. A specific person normally takes a before them: veo a Marta correr. The observed person or thing can also follow the action verb, especially when it is new information.

example.en: I see Marta run.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a specific person as the object
cards.noteEn: Spanish generally places a before a specific person who receives a verb’s action. This “personal a” is not translated as a separate English word.

example.en: I see Marta.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.

example.en: I know Marta.

cards.noteEn: Caerse describes a person or thing losing balance or falling, without naming someone who makes it fall. The attached se changes with the person in changed verb forms: me caigo, te caes, se cae.

example.en: The child may fall.

cards.promptEs: ser para identidad · estar para ubicación
cards.questionEn: Which Spanish “to be” verb says what something is, and which says where it is?
cards.answerEn: Use ser for identity or a defining description; use estar for the location of a person or thing.
cards.noteEn: This contrast is not simply permanent versus temporary. Forms of ser such as soy and es identify or describe what something is. Forms of estar such as están normally locate people and things. Events are a common exception: Spanish uses ser to say where or when an event takes place.

example.es: El museo es famoso y está en Madrid.
example.en: The museum is famous and is in Madrid.
